claim: A 10-year Treasury note held to maturity returns its face value plus coupons, but not its purchasing power. Buying at the monthly average 10-year yield in any month from April 1953 to August 2016 and holding for ten years (760 purchase months), the note lost to CPI-U inflation in 22.76% of cases, and in 51.46% of purchase months since 2008. All 30 of 30 purchase months from February 2014 to August 2016 lost purchasing power, averaging -0.86% a year after inflation (worst -1.77%), compared with the worst outcome on record (-2.53% a year for notes bought in late 1971).

numbers.definition: Purchase months s in the GS10 file (monthly average 10-year constant-maturity Treasury yield, percent) with s+120 months <= 2026-08 and CPIAUCNS (CPI-U all items, NSA) present at s and s+120; 2015-10 is dropped because CPI for 2025-10 is missing.

Share of purchase months whose realized real return r is negative, x100, where r = ((1 + GS10(s)/200)^20 / (CPIAUCNS(s+120)/CPIAUCNS(s)))^(1/10) - 1 (par note, semiannual coupons reinvested at the purchase yield).
Number of valid purchase months from 2014-02 to 2016-08 inclusive.
Number of those months with r < 0.
Minimum r over purchase months 2014-02..2016-08, x100.
Arithmetic mean of r over purchase months 2014-02..2016-08, x100.
Share of valid purchase months from 2008-01 onward with r < 0, x100.
Minimum r over all valid purchase months, x100.

assumptions: The note is bought at par at the monthly average constant-maturity yield of the purchase month and held 120 months; coupons are reinvested at the purchase yield (so the nominal result equals the yield to maturity), no taxes or fees.
Inflation over the holding period = CPI-U (NSA) at the maturity month divided by CPI-U at the purchase month.
